# Greater Prairie-Chicken

 Adult male. Photo: Steve Oehlenschlager/iStock 

 Adult male. Photo: Megumi Aita/Audubon Photography Awards 

 Adult males. Photo: Fi Rust/Audubon Photography Awards 

Tympanuchus cupido

 At a Glance Range & Identification Behavior Conservation Explore More Back to Top 

## At a Glance

 At one time, the eerie hollow moaning of the male Greater Prairie-Chickens displaying on their spring 'booming grounds' was a common sound across much of central and eastern North America. Today, both Greater Prairie-Chicken and Lesser Prairie-Chicken are quite uncommon and localized; the race on the Atlantic seaboard, called the Heath Hen, became extinct in 1932. Greater Prairie-Chickens still thrive on a few areas of native grassland in the midwest. 

 Category Phasianidae, Pheasants and Grouse, Upland Ground Birds 

 IUCN Status Vulnerable 

 Habitat 

 Fields, Meadows, and Grasslands, Shrublands, Savannas, and Thickets 

 Region Great Lakes, Plains, Rocky Mountains, Texas 

 Behavior Direct Flight, Flushes, Rapid Wingbeats, Running 

 Population 360.000 

## Range & Identification

### Migration & Range Maps

 Some individuals are permanent residents, others may move between breeding and wintering areas, traveling as much as 100 miles. No obvious or consistent differences in habitat between breeding and wintering sites. 

### Description

 Sexes similar; male slightly larger — Length: 16.1 - 18.9 in (41 - 48 cm); wingspan: 2 ft- 2 ft 4 in (61 - 71 cm); weight: 1 lb 11 oz- 2 lb 12 oz (750 g - 1.3 kg). The Greater Prairie-Chicken is chunky, brown, and heavily barred, especially on underparts. Male's yellow neck sacs are visible only in courtship display. In flight, shows short black tail. 

 Size 

 About the size of a Crow, About the size of a Mallard or Herring Gull 

 Color Black, Brown, Orange, Red, Tan, White, Yellow 

 Wing Shape Broad, Fingered, Rounded 

 Tail Shape Rounded, Short, Square-tipped 

### Songs and Calls

 Hollow "booming" call during display; also cackles and clucks. 

 Call Pattern Flat 

 Call Type Drum, Odd, Scream 

### Habitat

 Native tall-grass prairie. Prime original habitat apparently was where prairie was intermixed with oak woodland. Currently found in areas of tall-grass prairie (especially native prairie, which is now rare), including places where such habitat is interspersed with agricultural fields. 

## Behavior

### Eggs

 A Greater Prairie-Chicken usually lays 10-12 eggs, sometimes 7-17. The eggs are olive to pale buff, speckled with dark brown. Incubation is by female only, 23-25 days. 

### Young

 Follow female away from nest shortly after hatching. Young find all their own food. Can make short flights at about two weeks, stronger flights at three weeks. Young usually remain with female for almost three months. 

### Feeding Behavior

 Forages mostly on the ground, occasionally in trees. Most feeding in early morning and evening. 

### Diet

 The winter diet of a Greater Prairie-Chicken is mostly leaves and seeds, also waste grain in agricultural fields. Historically, may have eaten many acorns in winter, and still may do so where they are available. In summer eats a variety of leaves, buds, seeds, berries, and insects. Young birds eat more insects. 

### Nesting

 In spring, males gather on "booming grounds" and display there to attract females. Booming ground often on low hill, with good visibility; typically 8-20 males present, exceptionally up to 70. In display, male lowers head and raises tail, inflates air sacs on neck, raises feather tufts, stamps feet rapidly while making hollow moaning sounds; may leap in the air with loud cackles. Female visits booming ground, mates with one of the males. Nest site is on ground, among thick tall grass. Nest (built by female) is shallow depression lined with grass, leaves, feathers. 

## Conservation

### Conservation Status

 Atlantic Coast race (Heath Hen) became extinct in 1932; Texas coast race (Attwater's) is seriously endangered. Loss of habitat is single greatest threat to remaining Greater Prairie-Chicken populations in interior.

 Audubon’s scientists have used 140 million bird observations and sophisticated climate models to project how climate change will affect the range of the Greater Prairie-Chicken. Learn even more in Audubon’s Survival By Degrees project.
